lessons.title: Fixing Grainy Chocolate and Candy
lessons.body: Grainy chocolate or candy happens when sugar or cocoa particles are too large. In Africa, humidity and coarse sugar are common causes. To fix grainy chocolate, you need to re-temper it. First, chop the chocolate finely. Melt two-thirds of it in a bowl over hot water (not above 50Â°C). Stir until smooth. Remove from heat and add the remaining chopped chocolate. Stir continuously until it cools to 31Â°C for dark chocolate or 29Â°C for milk chocolate. If you don't have a thermometer, drip a small amount on your lip â it should feel neither warm nor cool. If still grainy, repeat the melting and cooling process. For candy, like fudge or fondant, graininess comes from large sugar crystals. To fix, add 2 tablespoons of corn syrup or lemon juice per cup of sugar when cooking. Stir gently only until sugar dissolves, then stop stirring. Wash down sides of the pot with a wet pastry brush. If candy is already grainy, re-melt it with a little water (1 tablespoon per cup) and re-cook to the correct temperature. For hard candy, graininess can be prevented by using a candy thermometer and not stirring after boiling begins. In Africa, where sugar may be coarser, pulse it in a blender for 10 seconds before use. Always store chocolate at 18-20Â°C and 50-55% humidity. If you live in a humid area, keep chocolate in an airtight container with silica gel packets. For grainy candy that has set, you can sometimes save it by grinding it in a food processor and using it as a topping or in baked goods. But prevention is better: use fine sugar, control temperature, and avoid stirring once boiling starts.

lessons.title: Preventing Bloom on Chocolate in Heat
lessons.body: Bloom is the white, chalky coating on chocolate. It's not mold â it's either fat bloom (cocoa butter separates) or sugar bloom (moisture draws sugar to the surface). In hot African climates, fat bloom is common when chocolate is stored above 24Â°C. To prevent bloom, store chocolate in a cool, dark place. Ideal temperature is 18-20Â°C with humidity below 55%. If you don't have air conditioning, use a cooler box with a frozen water bottle wrapped in a towel. Never store chocolate in the fridge â condensation causes sugar bloom. If you must refrigerate, wrap tightly in plastic and let it come to room temperature before opening. For chocolate you've made, ensure it is properly tempered. Tempering aligns cocoa butter crystals so they are stable at higher temperatures. Test temper by dipping a knife tip in the chocolate and waiting 5 minutes at room temperature (around 27Â°C). It should set glossy and hard. If it streaked or stayed soft, re-temper. For already bloomed chocolate, you can fix it by re-melting and re-tempering. The bloom will disappear. If you're selling chocolate in a hot market, use insulated packaging. Add a small ice pack in a styrofoam box. For candy coatings, like chocolate-covered nuts, add 1% cocoa butter to the chocolate to make it more heat-resistant. In West Africa, some makers add a little shea butter to chocolate to raise the melting point, but this changes texture. Better to use proper tempering and cool storage. If you see bloom on stored chocolate, don't throw it away â it's safe to eat and can be used in baking or melted for sauces. But for selling, re-temper to restore shine.

lessons.title: Adjusting Recipes When Ingredients Change
lessons.body: Ingredients vary across Africa. Sugar from different brands may have different moisture. Cocoa beans from Ghana, Ivory Coast, or Nigeria have different fat content. Milk powder may be full-fat or skimmed. When you change an ingredient, you must adjust. Start by keeping a notebook. Record every batch: ingredient brand, weight, temperature, and result. If you switch from full-fat milk powder to skimmed, add 1 tablespoon of vegetable oil per cup of skimmed milk powder to replace missing fat. If your new cocoa powder is darker and more acidic, reduce baking soda by 1/4 teaspoon per cup and add a pinch more salt. For caramel, if you use brown sugar instead of white, reduce the liquid by 2 tablespoons per cup because brown sugar has more moisture. If your honey is thicker, warm it slightly before measuring. For chocolate, if you use cocoa butter from a different source, test tempering: melt a small batch and check setting time. If it takes longer than 5 minutes at 27Â°C, add 1% more cocoa butter. For candy, if glucose syrup is unavailable, substitute with golden syrup or honey, but reduce the sugar by 10% because these are sweeter and contain more water. Always cook candy to 2Â°C higher when using liquid sweeteners. When changing flour, if you use cassava flour instead of wheat, add 1/2 teaspoon xanthan gum per cup for binding. For chocolate molds, if you use local vegetable oil instead of cocoa butter, the chocolate will be softer â add 2% cocoa butter to harden. Test small batches before full production. If a recipe fails, don't throw it out â note what went wrong and adjust next time. In Africa, where supply is inconsistent, flexibility is key. Keep a backup supplier and always taste as you go.

lessons.title: Dealing with Sticky or Hard Caramels
lessons.body: Caramel problems come from temperature and sugar chemistry. Sticky caramel means you didn't cook it high enough. Hard caramel means you overcooked it. Use a candy thermometer. For soft, chewy caramels, cook to 118-120Â°C (firm ball stage). For hard caramels, cook to 150-155Â°C (hard crack stage). If you don't have a thermometer, test in cold water: drop a bit of caramel into a glass of cold water. If it forms a soft ball that flattens when removed, it's soft caramel. If it forms a hard thread, it's hard caramel. In Africa, humidity affects caramel. On rainy days, cook 2Â°C higher because moisture in the air can make caramel sticky. To fix sticky caramel, return it to the pot with 2 tablespoons of water per cup of caramel. Stir over low heat until melted, then re-cook to 120Â°C. To fix hard caramel, add 1-2 tablespoons of water or cream per cup and re-melt gently. For hard caramel that's too brittle, add 1 tablespoon of butter or oil per cup and stir until smooth. Always stir caramel constantly after it reaches 110Â°C to prevent burning. Use a heavy-bottomed pot. If your caramel is grainy, add 1 tablespoon of corn syrup per cup and re-melt. For sticky caramels that won't set, you can roll them in wax paper and store in the fridge â they'll firm up. For hard caramels, break them into shards and use as topping. To prevent future problems, calibrate your thermometer in boiling water (100Â°C at sea level; adjust for altitude: subtract 1Â°C for every 300m above sea level). In high-altitude African cities like Nairobi (1,795m), water boils at about 94Â°C, so cook caramel to 6Â°C lower than the standard temperature. Always test a small batch first.

lessons.title: Salvaging Burnt Batches
lessons.body: Burnt chocolate or candy tastes bitter and smells acrid. But you can sometimes save it. For burnt chocolate, scrape off the burnt bottom and top layers. If the whole batch smells burnt, it's likely ruined â but you can use it in brownies or cakes where strong flavors mask the burn. For burnt caramel, immediately pour it into a clean pot, leaving the burnt part behind. Add 1 cup of water and 1 cup of sugar per 2 cups of burnt caramel. Stir over low heat until dissolved, then strain through a fine mesh. Re-cook to the desired temperature. The burnt flavor may be reduced but not eliminated. For burnt candy like brittle, break off the burnt edges and use the rest. If the entire batch is burnt, grind it into powder and use as a coffee substitute or in spice rubs. For burnt fudge, cut away burnt parts, then re-melt the rest with 1/4 cup of milk per 2 cups of fudge. Stir until smooth and re-set. To prevent burning, use a heavy pot and stir constantly. In Africa, where power outages are common, use a gas stove or charcoal stove with a diffuser plate to distribute heat evenly. Never leave candy unattended. If you smell burning, remove from heat immediately. For chocolate, melt in a double boiler, not direct heat. If you burn chocolate, don't add water â it will seize. Instead, add 1 teaspoon of vegetable oil per 100g and stir. If that fails, use it for baking. Always keep a backup batch of ingredients. If you burn a batch, don't panic â assess the damage. If it's only slightly burnt, you can mask it with vanilla or cinnamon. But if it's heavily burnt, discard it. The cost of ingredients is less than the cost of a bad reputation.

lessons.title: Repairing Broken Packaging and Molds
lessons.body: Broken packaging and molds cost money and ruin presentation. For chocolate bars that break, you can re-melt and re-mold. But if the break is clean, you can sell as 'chocolate pieces' at a discount. For cracked molds, if they are silicone, you can repair small tears with food-grade silicone sealant. Clean the mold with hot soapy water, dry completely, then apply sealant and let cure for 24 hours. For plastic molds, cracks cannot be repaired â replace them. In Africa, where molds may be expensive, consider making your own molds from food-grade silicone putty. Mix equal parts of silicone base and catalyst, press over a master shape (like a clean coin or carved wood), and let set for 2 hours. For broken packaging, like torn wrappers, use a heat sealer to reseal. If you don't have one, use a clothes iron on low heat with a sheet of parchment paper over the wrapper. Press for 3 seconds. For boxes, reinforce corners with tape. For labels that peel, use a glue stick or double-sided tape. To prevent breakage, store chocolate in rigid containers. For shipping, use bubble wrap or newspaper. In hot climates, avoid packaging that melts â use foil-lined bags. For molds that stick, lightly oil with coconut oil before pouring chocolate. If chocolate sticks, tap the mold on the counter to release. If it still sticks, place in the freezer for 5 minutes, then invert. For broken candy, like lollipops, you can re-melt on a silicone mat in the oven at 150Â°C for 5 minutes, then re-shape. Always keep spare packaging and molds. If you sell at markets, bring a repair kit: tape, scissors, extra wrappers, and a small iron. A little repair can save a whole batch.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of grainy chocolate?
options: A) Large sugar or cocoa particles
quiz.explanation: Graininess comes from large particles that haven't been refined enough.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you cool dark chocolate during tempering?
quiz.explanation: Dark chocolate is tempered when cooled to 31Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you fix grainy candy like fudge?
options: B) Re-melt with water and re-cook
quiz.explanation: Re-melting with a little water and re-cooking dissolves large crystals.

quiz.q: What is bloom on chocolate?
options: B) Fat or sugar crystals on surface
quiz.explanation: Bloom is either fat or sugar that has separated to the surface.

quiz.q: How should you store chocolate to prevent bloom in hot climates?
options: B) In a cooler box with ice pack
D) In a plastic bag on the counter
quiz.explanation: A cooler box with a frozen water bottle keeps chocolate cool without condensation.

quiz.q: What causes sugar bloom on chocolate?
quiz.explanation: Moisture draws sugar to the surface, causing sugar bloom.

quiz.q: How can you test if chocolate is properly tempered?
options: A) Dip a knife and wait 5 minutes
D) Put it in the fridge
quiz.explanation: A properly tempered chocolate sets glossy and hard within 5 minutes at room temperature.

quiz.q: What should you add to chocolate to make it more heat-resistant?
quiz.explanation: Adding 1% cocoa butter raises the melting point slightly.

quiz.q: When substituting skimmed milk powder for full-fat, what should you add?
quiz.explanation: Add 1 tablespoon of vegetable oil per cup to replace missing fat.

quiz.q: If you use brown sugar instead of white in caramel, what adjustment is needed?
options: B) Reduce liquid by 2 tbsp per cup
quiz.explanation: Brown sugar has more moisture, so reduce liquid to avoid stickiness.

quiz.q: What is a good substitute for glucose syrup in candy?
quiz.explanation: Honey or golden syrup can replace glucose, but reduce sugar by 10%.

quiz.q: When using cassava flour instead of wheat, what should you add for binding?
quiz.explanation: Xanthan gum helps bind gluten-free flours.

quiz.q: What temperature should soft, chewy caramels be cooked to?
quiz.explanation: 118-120Â°C is the firm ball stage for soft caramels.

quiz.q: How can you fix sticky caramel?
quiz.explanation: Re-melting with water and re-cooking to the right temperature fixes stickiness.

quiz.q: Why should you cook caramel 2Â°C higher on rainy days?
quiz.explanation: Humidity adds moisture, so higher cooking temperature compensates.

quiz.q: What is the boiling point of water in Nairobi (1,795m altitude)?
quiz.explanation: At 1,795m, water boils at about 94Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you salvage burnt chocolate?
quiz.explanation: Burnt chocolate can be masked in strongly flavored baked goods.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately if you smell burning candy?
quiz.explanation: Removing from heat stops further burning.

quiz.q: What can you add to burnt caramel to reduce burnt flavor?
options: A) Water and sugar, then re-cook
quiz.explanation: Re-cooking with water and sugar dilutes the burnt taste.

quiz.q: How can you repair a small tear in a silicone mold?
quiz.explanation: Food-grade silicone sealant is safe and flexible.

quiz.q: What can you use to make your own chocolate molds?
quiz.explanation: Silicone putty is food-safe and easy to shape.

quiz.q: How can you reseal a torn wrapper without a heat sealer?
options: A) Use a clothes iron on low with parchment
quiz.explanation: A clothes iron on low heat can melt the wrapper closed.

quiz.q: What should you do if chocolate sticks in a mold?
quiz.explanation: Tapping helps release air bubbles and loosen chocolate.

quiz.q: How can you re-shape broken lollipops?
options: A) Melt in oven at 150Â°C for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Low oven heat softens candy for re-shaping.

quiz.q: What is a key prevention for grainy candy?
options: B) Use fine sugar and avoid stirring after boiling
quiz.explanation: Fine sugar and minimal stirring prevent large crystal formation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage humidity for chocolate?
quiz.explanation: 50-55% humidity prevents sugar bloom.

quiz.q: What should you do if your caramel is too hard?
options: A) Add water or cream and re-melt
quiz.explanation: Adding liquid and re-melting softens hard caramel.

quiz.q: What is a sign of properly tempered chocolate?
options: A) Glossy and hard at room temperature
quiz.explanation: Tempered chocolate sets glossy and hard.

quiz.q: How can you prevent bloom when shipping chocolate?
options: A) Use insulated packaging with ice pack
quiz.explanation: Insulation and ice packs keep chocolate cool during transit.

quiz.q: What should you do if you burn a batch of fudge?
options: A) Cut away burnt parts and re-melt rest with milk
quiz.explanation: Salvage unburnt parts by re-melting with milk.
